$\operatorname{rank}(A)$ equals the number of pivots (nonzero rows) of $U$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Row operations are invertible left multiplications, so by the argument of @lem-invertible-preserves-rank
applied to $A^\top$ they do not change the row space: the rows of $U$ and the rows of $A$ span the same
subspace $\mathcal{C}(A^\top)$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$. (Each row of $U$ is a linear combination of rows of $A$
and vice versa, since the operations are reversible.) Hence the nonzero rows of $U$ span
$\mathcal{C}(A^\top)$.

They are also independent. Suppose $\mathbf{u}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{u}^{(s)}$ are the nonzero rows, with
the pivot of $\mathbf{u}^{(t)}$ in column $p_t$, where $p_1<p_2<\dots<p_s$ by the echelon staircase.
Suppose $\sum_{t=1}^s c_t\mathbf{u}^{(t)}=\mathbf{0}$. Look at column $p_1$, the leftmost pivot column:
only $\mathbf{u}^{(1)}$ has a nonzero entry there (every later row has zeros in all columns up to and
including its predecessors' pivots, in particular in column $p_1$), so the $p_1$-entry of the combination
is $c_1\,U_{1,p_1}=0$ with $U_{1,p_1}\neq 0$, forcing $c_1=0$. With $c_1=0$, repeat at column $p_2$ to get
$c_2=0$, and so on; all $c_t=0$. Thus the nonzero rows are independent and form a basis of
$\mathcal{C}(A^\top)$, whose dimension is $\operatorname{rank}(A^\top)=\operatorname{rank}(A)$ by
@thm-row-rank-column-rank. The number of nonzero rows is the number $s$ of pivots. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This is the practical face of rank. To find how many independent effects a design
can resolve, run elimination and count pivots; the pivot columns name a non-redundant set of model
columns, and the free (non-pivot) columns are exactly the redundant ones responsible for any
non-identifiability. The next time software reports a "rank-deficient model matrix," it has found fewer
pivots than columns.

## Characterizations of invertibility {#sec-la1-invertibility}

A square matrix is invertible when it has a two-sided multiplicative inverse. For square matrices a
remarkable collapse occurs: a long list of a priori distinct conditions, about solutions, columns, rank,
and one-sided inverses, are all equivalent. This theorem is used constantly, for instance to certify that
the normal-equations matrix $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ of regression can be inverted.

::: {#def-invertible}
## Invertible matrix
A matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is **invertible** (or *nonsingular*) if there exists
$B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ with $AB=BA=I_n$. Such a $B$ is unique when it exists: if $AB=BA=I_n$ and
$AB'=B'A=I_n$ then $B=BI_n=B(AB')=(BA)B'=I_nB'=B'$. We write $B=A^{-1}$.
:::

**What this means.** "Invertible" means the matrix can be perfectly undone: $A^{-1}$ exactly reverses
what $A$ does, so $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ can always be solved by $\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$. The
synonym *nonsingular* means precisely the same thing; this book uses "invertible" throughout, and the two
words may be read interchangeably whenever a source you consult prefers the other.

The next theorem lists ten conditions that are all equivalent to invertibility. That is a lot to hold in
mind at once, so before the statement here is a map. The conditions fall into four groups that say the
same thing in four languages, and the proof links the groups along a short cycle of implications.

| Group | Conditions | What the group says |
|---|---|---|
| Inverse conditions | (1), (2), (3), (10) | a genuine inverse exists (two-sided, or one-sided; and $A^\top$ inverts too) |
| Rank conditions | (4), (5), (6), (7) | the columns are independent and span; the rank is full |
| Solution conditions | (8), (9) | every system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution; the map is a bijection |

The proof establishes the arrows in the following table; together they form cycles that link all ten
conditions, so any one implies every other.

| Implication proved | Role |
|---|---|
| (4) $\Leftrightarrow$ (5) $\Leftrightarrow$ (7) $\Leftrightarrow$ (6) | the rank group is internally equivalent |
| (4),(6) $\Leftrightarrow$ (9) $\Leftrightarrow$ (8) | ties the rank group to the solution group |
| (9) $\Rightarrow$ (1) | a bijection has a linear inverse matrix |
| (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2) and (1) $\Rightarrow$ (3) | a genuine inverse is in particular one-sided |
| (2) $\Rightarrow$ (4) | a left inverse kills the null space |
| (3) $\Rightarrow$ (6) | a right inverse forces the columns to span |
| (1) $\Leftrightarrow$ (10) | transpose |

::: {#thm-invertibility-characterization}
## Characterizations of invertibility
For a square matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, the following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is invertible.
2. $A$ has a left inverse: $BA=I_n$ for some $B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$.
3. $A$ has a right inverse: $AC=I_n$ for some $C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$.
4. $\mathcal{N}(A)=\{\mathbf{0}\}$; equivalently $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution.
5. The columns of $A$ are linearly independent.
6. The columns of $A$ span $\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, $\mathcal{C}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n$.
7. $\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$ ($A$ has full rank).
8. For every $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has a unique solution.
9. The linear map $T_A\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is a bijection.
10. $A^\top$ is invertible.

Each of these is moreover equivalent to $\det(A)\neq 0$; we take this last equivalence from the theory of
determinants (@strang2016, Chapter 5) rather than reproving it here.
:::

::: {.proof}
We first establish the equivalence of (4) through (9), which is pure rank-nullity, and then close the
loop through the inverse conditions (1), (2), (3), and (10).

*(4) $\Leftrightarrow$ (5) $\Leftrightarrow$ (7) $\Leftrightarrow$ (6).* By @prp-system-solvability(3),
$\mathcal{N}(A)=\{\mathbf{0}\}$ is the same statement as the columns being independent, giving
(4) $\Leftrightarrow$ (5). The matrix rank-nullity theorem @thm-rank-nullity for the square $A$ reads
$\operatorname{rank}(A)+\dim\mathcal{N}(A)=n$, so $\mathcal{N}(A)=\{\mathbf{0}\}$ if and only if
$\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$, giving (4) $\Leftrightarrow$ (7). Finally
$\operatorname{rank}(A)=\dim\mathcal{C}(A)$ and $\mathcal{C}(A)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, so
$\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$ if and only if $\mathcal{C}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n$ (a subspace of full dimension is
the whole space), giving (7) $\Leftrightarrow$ (6).

*(4),(6) $\Leftrightarrow$ (9) $\Leftrightarrow$ (8).* The map $T_A$ is injective if and only if
$\ker T_A=\mathcal{N}(A)=\{\mathbf{0}\}$ (@lem-injective-trivial-kernel), that is, condition (4); it is
surjective if and only if $\operatorname{im}T_A=\mathcal{C}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, condition (6).
Hence $T_A$ is bijective, condition (9), if and only if both (4) and (6) hold; but we have just shown (4)
and (6) are equivalent to each other, so any one of them is equivalent to (9). Bijectivity of $T_A$ is the
statement that $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution for each $\mathbf{b}$, condition (8).
Thus (8) $\Leftrightarrow$ (9).

*(9) $\Rightarrow$ (1).* If $T_A$ is a bijection it has an inverse function
$T_A^{-1}\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$. This inverse is linear: for
$\mathbf{u}=T_A\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{v}=T_A\mathbf{y}$,
$T_A^{-1}(a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v})=T_A^{-1}\big(T_A(a\mathbf{x}+b\mathbf{y})\big)=a\mathbf{x}+b\mathbf{y}
=a\,T_A^{-1}\mathbf{u}+b\,T_A^{-1}\mathbf{v}$. By @prp-matrices-are-maps it is $T_B$ for a matrix
$B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$. Then $T_A\circ T_B=T_B\circ T_A=\mathrm{id}$, and by
@thm-matrix-mult-composition this says $AB=BA=I_n$. So $A$ is invertible.

*(1) $\Rightarrow$ (2) and (1) $\Rightarrow$ (3).* Immediate: $A^{-1}$ is both a left and a right inverse.

*(2) $\Rightarrow$ (4).* Suppose $BA=I_n$. If $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ then
$\mathbf{x}=I_n\mathbf{x}=BA\mathbf{x}=B\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}$, so $\mathcal{N}(A)=\{\mathbf{0}\}$.

*(3) $\Rightarrow$ (6).* Suppose $AC=I_n$. For any $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^n$,
$A(C\mathbf{b})=(AC)\mathbf{b}=I_n\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}$, so $\mathbf{b}\in\mathcal{C}(A)$; hence
$\mathcal{C}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n$.

These implications close the loop. Indeed (2) $\Rightarrow$ (4) $\Rightarrow$ (9) $\Rightarrow$ (1)
$\Rightarrow$ (2), so (1), (2), (4), (9) are equivalent; and (3) $\Rightarrow$ (6) $\Rightarrow$ (9)
$\Rightarrow$ (1) $\Rightarrow$ (3), folding in (3). Together with the chain of the first two paragraphs,
all of (1) through (9) are equivalent.

*(1) $\Leftrightarrow$ (10).* If $AB=BA=I_n$, transpose: $B^\top A^\top=A^\top B^\top=I_n^\top=I_n$, so
$A^\top$ is invertible with $(A^\top)^{-1}=(A^{-1})^\top$. The converse applies the same to $A^\top$,
whose transpose is $A$. (Equivalently, $\operatorname{rank}(A^\top)=\operatorname{rank}(A)$ by
@thm-row-rank-column-rank, so $A$ has full rank if and only if $A^\top$ does, conditions (7) for each.)
$\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This theorem is the workhorse behind "the treatment effect is uniquely estimable."
In Chapter 6 the least-squares coefficients solve
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}$, which has a unique solution exactly
when the $p\times p$ matrix $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is invertible, that is (condition 7) when it has
full rank, which Exercise @exr-la1-gram-rank shows happens precisely when $\mathbf{X}$ has full column
rank. So "the columns of the design are independent" (no dummy-variable trap) and "the treatment effect
has a unique estimate" are, through this chain of equivalences, the same statement.

::: {.remark}
Two observations sharpen the theorem. First, for *square* matrices a one-sided inverse is automatically
two-sided: if $BA=I_n$ then, by the proof, $A$ is invertible, and
$B=B(AA^{-1})=(BA)A^{-1}=A^{-1}$, so $B$ is the genuine inverse; symmetrically for a right inverse. This
is special to square matrices and fails for rectangular ones. Second, the determinant condition links to
the spectral theory of Chapter 3: $A$ is invertible if and only if $0$ is not an eigenvalue, because
$\mathcal{N}(A)\neq\{\mathbf{0}\}$ is exactly the existence of a nonzero $\mathbf{x}$ with
$A\mathbf{x}=0\cdot\mathbf{x}$. The singular value decomposition @thm-svd makes the same statement through
singular values: $A$ is invertible if and only if all $n$ singular values are positive.
:::
## A worked example: the two-arm design matrix {#sec-la1-design-example}

We close by analyzing in full the very matrix that opened the chapter in @sec-la1-preview, now with every
tool in hand. The computation can be verified entirely by hand and previews the regression machinery of
Chapter 6. Recall the tiny clinical comparison: four patients, the first two on control and the last two
on an active treatment. We model an outcome with an intercept (a common baseline) and a treatment
indicator. The design matrix, with first column the intercept $\mathbf{1}_4$ and second column the
treatment indicator $\mathbf{t}=(0,0,1,1)^\top$, is
$$
\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\\1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 2},
\qquad
\boldsymbol\beta=\begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\beta_1\end{pmatrix},
$$
so that $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_0,\beta_0+\beta_1,\beta_0+\beta_1)^\top$: every control
patient is predicted to have outcome $\beta_0$ and every treated patient $\beta_0+\beta_1$, making
$\beta_1$ the treatment effect.

::: {#exm-design-matrix}
## Four subspaces of a two-arm design
We compute, for the matrix $\mathbf{X}$ above (here $m=4$, $n=p=2$), all four fundamental subspaces, the
rank, and the consequences for solving $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{y}$.

**Rank.** The two columns $\mathbf{1}_4$ and $\mathbf{t}$ are not scalar multiples of each other, so they
are linearly independent and $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X})=2$. As $n=p=2$, the matrix has *full column
rank*.

**Column space.** $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{1}_4,\mathbf{t}\}\subseteq
\mathbb{R}^4$ is two-dimensional. A vector $\mathbf{v}=(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4)^\top$ lies in it if and only if
$\mathbf{v}=\beta_0\mathbf{1}_4+\beta_1\mathbf{t}$ for some scalars, that is, $v_1=v_2=\beta_0$ and
$v_3=v_4=\beta_0+\beta_1$. So the column space is exactly the set of vectors that are *constant within
each treatment group*.

**Null space.** Solve $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{0}$. Reading the rows,
$\beta_0=0$ and $\beta_0+\beta_1=0$, hence $\beta_0=\beta_1=0$. Thus
$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})=\{\mathbf{0}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$, of dimension $0$. Rank-nullity checks out:
$\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X})+\dim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})=2+0=2=p$.

**Row space.** $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ is spanned by the rows $(1,0)$ and
$(1,1)$ (the distinct rows of $\mathbf{X}$). These are independent, so the row space is all of
$\mathbb{R}^2$, of dimension $2=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X})$, as @thm-four-subspaces requires.

**Left null space.** By @eq-four-dims its dimension is $m-r=4-2=2$. A vector
$\mathbf{y}=(y_1,y_2,y_3,y_4)^\top$ lies in $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$ if and only if it is orthogonal
to both columns: $\mathbf{1}_4^\top\mathbf{y}=y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4=0$ and
$\mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{y}=y_3+y_4=0$. The second equation gives $y_4=-y_3$, and substituting into the
first gives $y_1+y_2=0$, so $y_2=-y_1$. Hence
$$
\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top)=\operatorname{span}\Big\{(1,-1,0,0)^\top,\ (0,0,1,-1)^\top\Big\},
$$
the *within-group mean-zero contrasts*. One verifies directly that each basis vector is orthogonal to
$\mathbf{1}_4$ and to $\mathbf{t}$, confirming $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top)=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp$
of @eq-four-orth.

**Solvability.** By @prp-system-solvability(1), $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{y}$ has a solution if
and only if $\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$, that is, if and only if $y_1=y_2$ and $y_3=y_4$. Real
outcome data almost never satisfy this, which is the whole reason we *project* the data onto
$\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ and solve in the least-squares sense; that projection is the subject of
Chapter 2, and the resulting estimator is the ordinary least squares estimator of Chapter 6. When a
solution does exist it is unique here, because $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})=\{\mathbf{0}\}$
(@prp-system-solvability(3)).

**The normal-equations matrix.** Anticipating Chapter 6, compute the Gram matrix
$$
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{1}_4^\top\mathbf{1}_4 & \mathbf{1}_4^\top\mathbf{t}\\
\mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{1}_4 & \mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{t}\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \det(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=4\cdot 2-2\cdot 2=4\neq 0 .
$$
Because $\det\neq 0$, the matrix is invertible by @thm-invertibility-characterization, with
$$
(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12 & -\tfrac12\\[2pt] -\tfrac12 & 1\end{pmatrix}.
$$
(One checks $\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12&-\tfrac12\\-\tfrac12&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ by hand.) The invertibility of $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is no
accident: it holds exactly because $\mathbf{X}$ has full column rank, the equivalence proved in general in
Exercise @exr-la1-gram-rank. This is the precise condition under which the regression coefficients, and
hence the treatment effect $\beta_1$, are uniquely estimable. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
## Collinearity and non-identifiability
Suppose we had instead included a redundant third column, the control indicator
$\mathbf{c}=(1,1,0,0)^\top=\mathbf{1}_4-\mathbf{t}$, forming
$\mathbf{X}'=[\mathbf{1}_4\ \ \mathbf{t}\ \ \mathbf{c}]\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 3}$. Now the columns satisfy
the linear dependence $\mathbf{1}_4-\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0}$, so
$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}')\ni(1,-1,-1)^\top\neq\mathbf{0}$ and one computes
$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}')=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1,-1)^\top\}$, of dimension $1$. By rank-nullity
$\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}')=3-1=2$: adding the column did not raise the rank. Consequently
$\mathbf{X}'^\top\mathbf{X}'\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$ has rank $2<3$ and is *not* invertible, so the
normal equations no longer pin down a unique coefficient vector. Concretely, as computed in
@exm-la1-nonidentifiability, the distinct coefficient vectors $(0,1,0)^\top$ and $(1,0,-1)^\top$ produce
the identical fitted values $(0,0,1,1)^\top$, so no data can choose between them. This is the "dummy
variable trap": the intercept and the two group indicators are collinear, and the treatment effect is
identifiable only as the contrast $\beta_{\text{trt}}-\beta_{\text{ctrl}}$, a linear functional that is
constant along the null direction $(1,-1,-1)^\top$. The remedy practiced everywhere in this book, dropping
one indicator, is exactly the restoration of full column rank. Identifiability in indirect comparison is,
at bottom, this same statement about null spaces.
:::
## Notes and references {#sec-la1-notes}

The development of vector spaces, bases, and dimension through the Steinitz exchange theorem
(@thm-steinitz-exchange) is classical and is treated in any linear-algebra text; we follow the spirit of
@strang2016, the standard reference for the applied theory and the origin of the "four fundamental
subspaces" organizing picture (@def-column-space, @thm-four-subspaces). The rank factorization
@eq-rank-factorization used to prove that row rank equals column rank (@thm-row-rank-column-rank) is
standard; the proof given here is self-contained. The rank-nullity theorem (@thm-rank-nullity) is the
load-bearing result of the chapter and is proved in full; everything in later chapters that counts
degrees of freedom, from the residual degrees of freedom of regression to the dimension of an estimable
contrast space, is an application of it.

We have stated the orthogonality of the four subspaces (@eq-four-orth) and proved the elementary
set-equalities, but deferred the projection geometry that realizes the orthogonal decomposition
$\mathbb{R}^n=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)\oplus\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})$ to the orthogonal projection
theorem @thm-projection-theorem and the Gram-Schmidt construction @thm-gram-schmidt of Chapter 2. The
existence and algorithm of (reduced) row-echelon form, used in @prp-rank-equals-pivots, and the
determinant characterization of invertibility in @thm-invertibility-characterization, are taken from
@strang2016 rather than reproved; full determinant theory is not needed in this book beyond this one
equivalence, and the eigenvalue and singular-value characterizations of invertibility are returned to in
Chapter 3 (@thm-spectral-theorem, @thm-svd, @thm-pd-characterization). The design-matrix example of
@sec-la1-design-example is the seed of the linear-model theory developed from first principles in
Chapter 6 (@def-linear-model, @thm-ols-normal-equations, @def-hat-matrix); the invertibility of
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ under full column rank, previewed there and proved in Exercise
@exr-la1-gram-rank, is the algebraic precondition for the existence and uniqueness of the least-squares
estimator.

This chapter has no counterpart in the `ITC_Coq` development and therefore carries no machine-checked
tags.

## Exercises {#sec-la1-exercises}

Exercises marked with a star ($\star$) have a full worked solution in Appendix F. The tag after each
title flags its flavor: *warm-up* and *interpretation* exercises need only the ideas, not heavy
algebra, and are the place to start; *computation* exercises ask you to grind a small example by hand;
*proof* and *starred challenge* exercises build machinery used later in the book. Begin with the
warm-ups, which use the running two-arm trial of @sec-la1-preview.

::: {#exr-la1-warmup-fitted}
## Fitted values by hand (warm-up)
Using the running two-arm design
$\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\\1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ of @sec-la1-preview and the coefficient
vector $\boldsymbol\beta=(5,3)^\top$: (a) compute the fitted-value vector $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta$ by
hand. (b) Which patients share a predicted outcome, and why? (c) What is the predicted treatment effect,
that is, the predicted treated outcome minus the predicted control outcome?
:::

::: {#exr-la1-warmup-redundant}
## Spotting a redundant column (warm-up)
Consider the three columns $\mathbf{1}_4=(1,1,1,1)^\top$, $\mathbf{t}=(0,0,1,1)^\top$, and
$\mathbf{c}=(1,1,0,0)^\top$. (a) Write $\mathbf{c}$ as a linear combination of $\mathbf{1}_4$ and
$\mathbf{t}$. (b) Explain in one sentence why a design built from all three columns has rank $2$, not
$3$. (c) In plain words, what goes wrong if you try to estimate a separate intercept, control effect, and
treatment effect from these three columns?
:::

::: {#exr-la1-interpret-estimable}
## Which effect can you estimate? (interpretation)
A trialist fits an outcome model with an intercept, a control-group indicator, and a treatment-group
indicator, and is surprised the software cannot return unique estimates of the three coefficients. (a)
Identify the null-space direction responsible (see @sec-la1-identifiability). (b) Explain which single
quantity built from the coefficients *is* determined by the data, and why, referring to
@exm-la1-nonidentifiability. (c) State the one-line fix and say what, if anything, is lost.
:::

::: {#exr-la1-four-subspaces-compute}
## Computing the four subspaces (computation)
Let
$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\2&4&3\\3&6&4\end{pmatrix}.
$$
(a) Show that $\operatorname{rank}(A)=2$ by exhibiting a dependence among the rows and among the columns.
(b) Find a basis and the dimension of each of $\mathcal{C}(A)$, $\mathcal{C}(A^\top)$, $\mathcal{N}(A)$,
and $\mathcal{N}(A^\top)$. (c) Verify the dimension counts of @thm-four-subspaces and check explicitly
that your null-space basis vector is orthogonal to your row-space basis vectors.
:::

::: {#exr-la1-elementary-rank}
## Rank by elimination (computation)
Bring the matrix $A$ of @exr-la1-four-subspaces-compute to reduced row-echelon form by elementary row
operations, and confirm that the number of pivots equals the rank you found, as guaranteed by
@prp-rank-equals-pivots. Use the pivot columns to read off a basis of $\mathcal{C}(A)$ consisting of
columns of $A$. (Worked template: @exm-la1-elimination.)
:::

::: {#exr-la1-subspace-intersection}
## Intersections, unions, and sums of subspaces (proof)
Let $U$ and $W$ be subspaces of a vector space $V$. (a) Prove that $U\cap W$ is a subspace. (b) Give an
explicit example of two subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose union is not a subspace. (c) Prove that the sum
$U+W=\{\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}:\mathbf{u}\in U,\ \mathbf{w}\in W\}$ is a subspace, and is the smallest
subspace containing $U\cup W$.
:::

::: {#exr-la1-design-collinear}
## The dummy-variable trap (computation and interpretation)
For the augmented design $\mathbf{X}'=[\mathbf{1}_4\ \ \mathbf{t}\ \ \mathbf{c}]$ of the remark in
@sec-la1-design-example, with $\mathbf{t}=(0,0,1,1)^\top$ and $\mathbf{c}=(1,1,0,0)^\top$: (a) verify that
$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}')=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1,-1)^\top\}$; (b) compute
$\mathbf{X}'^\top\mathbf{X}'$ and show it is singular by exhibiting a nonzero vector in its null space;
(c) explain, using @prp-system-solvability, why the individual coefficients are not identifiable while the
contrast $\beta_{\mathbf{t}}-\beta_{\mathbf{c}}$ is.
:::

::: {#exr-la1-rank-product}
## Rank of a product (proof)
Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$. (a) Prove that
$\mathcal{C}(AB)\subseteq\mathcal{C}(A)$ and $\mathcal{N}(B)\subseteq\mathcal{N}(AB)$. (b) Deduce
$\operatorname{rank}(AB)\le\min\{\operatorname{rank}(A),\operatorname{rank}(B)\}$. (c) Show that if $A$ has
full column rank (its columns independent) then $\operatorname{rank}(AB)=\operatorname{rank}(B)$, and if
$B$ has full row rank then $\operatorname{rank}(AB)=\operatorname{rank}(A)$.
:::

::: {#exr-la1-rank-one}
## Rank-one matrices (proof)
Let $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonzero. (a) Prove that the outer
product $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ has rank exactly $1$, and describe its column
space and row space. (b) Conversely, prove that every matrix of rank $1$ can be written as
$\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top$ for some nonzero $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}$. (Hint for (b): a rank-one matrix has
a one-dimensional column space spanned by some $\mathbf{u}$; express each column as a multiple of
$\mathbf{u}$.)
:::

::: {#exr-la1-left-right-inverse}
## One-sided inverses of a square matrix (proof)
Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$. Prove directly from @thm-invertibility-characterization that if $A$ has
a right inverse $C$ with $AC=I_n$, then $A$ is invertible and $C=A^{-1}$. Then give a $2\times 3$ matrix
$A$ and a $3\times 2$ matrix $C$ with $AC=I_2$ but $CA\neq I_3$, showing that the square hypothesis is
essential.
:::

::: {#exr-la1-map-unique-matrix}
## Linear maps are matrices (proof)
Without appealing to @prp-matrices-are-maps, prove from @lem-map-determined-by-basis that every linear map
$T\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ equals $T_A$ for a unique $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, and identify
the columns of $A$. Then prove that $T$ is injective if and only if the columns of $A$ are independent,
and surjective if and only if they span $\mathbb{R}^m$.
:::

::: {#exr-la1-dim-sum}
## Dimension of a sum (starred challenge)
$\star$ Let $U$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional subspaces of a vector space $V$. Prove the dimension formula
$$
\dim(U+W)=\dim U+\dim W-\dim(U\cap W).
$$
(Hint: start from a basis of $U\cap W$ and extend it, using @lem-basis-extension, to a basis of $U$ and
separately to a basis of $W$; prove that the combined list is a basis of $U+W$.) A solution appears in
Appendix F.
:::

::: {#exr-la1-gram-rank}
## The Gram matrix and full column rank (starred challenge)
$\star$ Let $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$. (a) Prove that
$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})$. (Hint: if
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$, consider
$\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\|_2^2$.) (b) Deduce that
$\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X})$, and hence that the
$p\times p$ Gram matrix $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is invertible if and only if $\mathbf{X}$ has full
column rank $p$. (c) Conclude that the normal-equations system
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}$ has a unique solution exactly when
$\mathbf{X}$ has full column rank, the algebraic foundation of ordinary least squares developed in
Chapter 6. A solution appears in Appendix F.
:::
